projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Helen Lanier was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Today is Friday, November 24, 2006, and I'm in Chadbourn, North Carolina interviewing Helen Lanier, born August 31, 1924. My name is Claire Lanier. Helen Lanier is my grandmother on my father's side.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Grandma, during what war were you involved in the civil service?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: World War II.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: And what year did you join the civil service?

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: And how old...oh, no, no, continue, I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I was in until 1945.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: And what year, how old were you when you joined?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Eighteen.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Eighteen. Okay well, let's just backtrack a little bit to before your time during the war. Where were you born?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I was born in Mahnomen County, Minnesota.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: And where did you grow up?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: In that same, same vicinity and went to several one-room schoolhouses where they had all eight grades in one room and one teacher, and then I went to the county high school in Mahnomen.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: And did you graduate from high school?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Yes, I did. I graduated with honors. I was third in my class of fifty-five.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Um, what did you, upon graduating, what did you, what were you thinking, what were your plans upon graduating?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I felt like I had to go to work because I had to have a job.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: What college an option for you?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I didn't think so at the time, although I did find out that I had won a scholarship, but, which I did not take advantage of cause I was not financially able to do it.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: I see. So what kind of work did you look for, or what work did you find, rather?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I found work as a waitress to start with. Then, I went to Council Bluffs, Iowa, to help my grandmother in a grocery store that she owned there so that her grandchildren that she had raised could finish their last year of high school. And it was there that I went to a radio school, and that's where I became involved with communications, Morse code, and could do that and intended to go into communications with civil service.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: What, how did that come about? How did you start partaking in those training programs?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Well it was mid-year and so, and that class came open so I just went to communications class.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: What did you, how long was that class?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: It was supposed to be a six-month class, but I only went three months.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Did you complete it?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I completed it and passed it.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Um, and after you passed that exam, where did that put you? Were you, I mean, what kind of job could you get with that?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Well, my intentions were to go with communications in some type. It wasn't military, but at that time they had civilians in communications at the different army bases and military in United States.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Um, in Council Bluffs, what, how long did you live there total?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Almost a year.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Did you have any friends there?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Um, my grandmother was there, and I had three cousins that were just a little younger than I was, and so I enjoyed my stay there. I did not really know my grandmother before I went there. I did get acquainted with her while I was there.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: What would you do in Council Bluffs when you weren't training or working at the grocery store?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: We mostly went to Omaha to concerts and different entertainment that they had in Omaha, Nebraska.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: What kind of concerts?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Musical concerts.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Cool. Alright, so from Council Bluffs I know you ended up in Iowa, how did that happen?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I ended up in...

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: I mean, in Utah, I'm sorry, I misspoke.

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Well, after, I took the radio test for the school that I was going to in Iowa. Incidentally, I was the only one who passed the Morse code test. When we came back, my instructor said if you can pass this communication test, he said, you could pass a civil service test so he told me where to go to take the civil service test and, of course, I passed it. And another friend went with me, and she also passed it. She could pass the civil service test, but not the Morse code test so, we both went to, got assigned to Utah.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Were...

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: But while we were on the train going to Utah, the military closed all communications to civilians so we could not go into it so we, when we got there, all we could go into was what they called the Mechanic Learner Program.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: What is that?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: It was in Logan, Utah, which was at the state college there so we went from Ogden, Utah, to Logan, Utah, and got in the Mechanic Learner Class and that was how come I was being involved with mechanics on the World War II planes that had been in service, been damaged and everything, were brought back to this country for repairs.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: So what did you learn in that training?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: We learned all, we learned the nomenclature of the planes, what made them fly, how they had to be repaired, I mean how they had to be, everything safety, how important it was to repair them right to go back into service, which most of them did, and we were there for three months I think, if I remember right, then we were sent to Ogden, Utah, to Hillfield, and actually begin work.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: In Logan for training, where did you live?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: We lived in a one room apartment over the police station, and at that time, Logan, Utah, was almost a hundred percent Mormon and when they brought in these people to train for that and the servicemen where they were also trained for radar, which had just come out, and the radar school was there so they had a few select ones from all branches of the service training there at the same time.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Who did you live with?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: With whom did you live?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I lived with another girl. We had a one room apartment with one bed in it, a hot plate and almost a community bath cause all of us that lived on that floor had one bathroom

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: That sounds like college.

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Well, in a way it was college education for all of us cause it was the first time most of us had been away from home and there were some kids sixteen, seventeen years old that were working. I don't know whether they were in the civil service or not but at that time labor was so scarce that they hired the young and the old mainly cause that's all there was to hire.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: What did you, in Logan, what would you do for fun when you weren't in training, and also how much time was spent actually at training, was this like forty hours a week?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: It was forty hours a week, forty hours a week

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: So then on the weekend, what would you do there?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Well, I done mostly roller skating and dancing cause at that time nobody had cars because if you had cars, you couldn't get gas for them, you couldn't get tires for them, so we had to walk about a mile to even get to the college and I think we walked up 90-some steps to get up to our classroom.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Every day?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Every day. There was no place that we could afford to eat at up there so we had to take our lunch because we all went out there without any money. The government had paid our way out there to work. Most of them were just out of high school that were in that class and nobody had any money, until we got our first paycheck. It was really kind of fun and funny now, but it wasn't then.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: How much was your paycheck, do you remember?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I think we started off at eighty cent an hour, which was fairly good money at the time.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Did you find the training to be difficult?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: No, I had never found school difficult. Some of them did, but I never found it difficult.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Did you have any experience going in, in airplane mechanics?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: In what?

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: In airplane mechanics, had you ever done anything like that before?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Totally new?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Totally new. All I had ever seen of airplanes was them up in the sky.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Okay, so you were in Logan for about three months and then you moved back down to Ogden. What was the situation like there? Did you also live in an apartment?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: No. No, we lived in, at the time I got to Hillfield, it was not completed. They didn't have sidewalks built or all of the streets weren't built. The dormitories, as I look back, were rather crude, they were not decorated, but we did live in dormitories which had two stories and they were, the rooms were not big. There was two girls to a room, each one had a closet and each one had a small dresser, and there was an apartment on each side of the building and a hallway down the middle that had a community bath so...

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: So it was about like what you had before?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: But it was definitely an improvement over the one room apartment that we had, and they also had a cafeteria on the, where we lived and we had a recreation hall there that we could go to at nights.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Did you?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Oh yes, we went to that recreation hall almost every night.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: What did you do there?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: We danced and talked and played games, just had a good time. And there was definitely no air condition, and Utah summers can be hot. And they did have sandstorms where nothing kept the sand out. You just brushed it off, shook your clothes, and went home.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Wow, so during sandstorms, would everything maintain, would everything stay normal or did you have to shut down at all?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: No, we never had to shutdown 'cause the hangers withstood the sandstorms pretty good, and if they were too bad, we might have to go home, but other than that, I don't ever remember going home cause of a sandstorm. We went home once or twice cause of a snowstorm cause it got too icy to work, but all-in-all at that period in my life, it was kind of an adventure as well as a good paying job cause civil service paid good, and we had to work overtime every week so we got, made extra money that way, and the dormitories were something like four dollars a paycheck or something is all we had to pay for them and we ate in the cafeteria which was very reasonable. And we worked part of the time three shifts a day. I never had to work graveyard 'cause they quit that before I had had to work, but I did work swing shift and day shift.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: So tell me, then tell me like, give me a rundown on a typical day at the base.

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Well, we generally had to get up at around six o'clock, and we'd go over and get breakfast at the cafeteria most of the time before cause we had no place to eat on the base, no chance to get anything to eat, and if we didn't take our lunch, they did have a place over there if we were close enough to it, we could go get something to eat. Most of the time, we'd pick us up a sandwich at the cafeteria and took it to work with us so we'd have something to eat. And we had transportation which consisted of a tractor pulling an open trailer which everybody called "elephant trains" cause they were so slow but we could get a lot of people standing up in that open trailer, there was no place to sit down. And it was about a mile from the cafeteria to where we went to work, and they had strict identification to get to work, they would check very closely at the gate to get in. Then we'd go in and seems to me like we had a ten minute break in the morning and a ten minute break in the afternoon.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: And then, what would, what kind of duties would you have during the day?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Well, the hangers were designed into ten work stations. Station Zero was where we most people started off unless they had experience. You had to use a power washing hose and wash all the removable parts of the plane, plus wash the plane, which was very hard work, being under that pressurized hose. And you stayed there until you really learned the parts of a plane and what made it work. Then most of the time they transferred you to some other station on a plane. I went to Station One, which was where you change the deicer boots and cleaned out the anti-icing system. The anti-icing system had to be flushed out, I don't' remember what we flushed it out with but the deicer system was putting on new boots on the leading edge...

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: On the what?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: On the leading edge of the wings, and it would inflate and crack that ice off when it was in flight, but we didn't have any mechanical way to put it on, so we'd put one edge of it on with screws, with a plain old screwdriver, not a power screwdriver, just a plain old screwdriver, and then we'd have somebody with a wooden handle and a wire hook on it pull it tight enough over there until we could pop the screws through it and fasten it in the holes that were there, which was also very hard work, but once you got to where you could do it, it went pretty fast, but when you first started, it was hard. Then, let's see, I went to...they started me...let me get it in chronological order...I was made supervisor on that station. I worked I guess five or six and worked with a lot of the service men that were in transit that would come in and stay there for a few weeks or a few days, however long it took to get their plane back and ready, and they also helped us out off and on on the plane line if we had...they were specialists in something that'd come and help or we'd help them, too, of course. And then after that they formed a fighter plane repair shop in a different hanger which was the P-47s, see we had been working on the B-24s, which were the bombers. The P-47s were the fighter planes, and I was, I was transferred to that project. There was very few girls that got the opportunity to go to the fighter planes.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Why were you transferred there?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Because I was considered one of the better workers or one of them that could learn the fastest maybe...[microphone mishap]...fighter planes were real small planes. Fighter planes were real small planes, and the bombers were the big planes,

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Was that a pay raise?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Did you get a pay raise?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Did you when you became a supervisor of station...

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Yes, when I became a supervisor I did, but for the times, it was always a fairly good paying job.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: But, of course, we didn't have the civil services benefits because we were temporary.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Oh, I see.

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: It didn't count as time with the civil service, it was counted as time with civil service, but there was no benefits attached to it.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: So did anything ever go wrong? Could someone get hurt with, in working with the planes?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Just minor things was all I ever heard of.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Like what?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Maybe cut their hands or something, or injure their leg jumping out of a plane where they weren't supposed to.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Was there a hospital on the base?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: There was what they called an infirmary, if you had a cold or something, you could go there and get medicine, a sore throat, a minor cut, you were treated for over there.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Going back to the servicemen who were visiting, or rather not visiting, just staying temporarily, did you have a lot of interaction with them socially?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Yes, they could eat in our cafeteria if they would like, although they did have their own mess hall, but, you know, everybody likes a change, and [coughs] every so often they would have, have a dance up on the base, and [coughs] they would come up and get a bus load of girls to go up there cause some of the servicemen would have somebody to dance with cause at that time, there was very few women in the service. We had some WAGS and some WAVES that were stationed there, but there wasn't many of them and they weren't very popular at that time with the men in the services. I mean, seemed like the men thought it was no place for the women to be in the service cause that was, see they had never been until then.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: [Pause] Oh, how many, what was the ratio on base of men to women?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I really have no idea, I would say with the employees and all, with the employees and all, I'd say it was probably thirty percent, something like that cause there was a lot of women employees because there was no men to work.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Right. How many people roughly do you think were on the base?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I'd say between ten and fifteen thousand.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: There was a lot people who worked there. And there was also some servicemen that had been injured in the war that came back there to work, some of them had lost limbs, some of them were just injured to where they could not go back into military combat, but they could do certain types of work.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Going back quickly to the everyday life, what did you wear for working?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: We wore mostly pants, blue jeans, jackets, and long shirts. It was cold in the wintertime there cause see it was up in the mountains, and in the summertime, we just wore, we couldn't wear shorts, we had to wear long pants.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: But there was no standard uniform or anything?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: No, no standard uniform for civilians.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: I see. Did you feel any pressure, or rather what did you feel, how did you feel about working on planes that had returned from war?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Well, sometimes we would get very despondent over if we got a plane that we knew somebody had been killed in or if we had to clean up blood where they had been wounded, and we'd just always wondered who it was, you know, if it was somebody who knew, some of our friends because it wasn't...there was a lot of crewmen on those planes, you know, like in the B-24s and the whole front was glass which was where the bombardiers shot, was sitting, and he was an easy target. It just made you wonder, made you sad to think about cause you never knew if it was some of your friends that had been in that plane.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Were you told where the planes were coming back from?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Would you be able to, I mean you mentioned knowing if someone had died in the plane, would they, how much information were you given?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: No, we just imagined...

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Oh, oh, oh....

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: But mostly by the condition of the plane cause see you couldn't wash off the inside of the plane that well with a pressure washer, most of that had to be hand-done.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Did you enjoy working as a mechanic?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Yes, I enjoyed it, it was something different, something I had never done, and I was young and adventurous. I probably would not enjoy it a bit after I got older, but I still keep in touch with some of the friends I had there, and they all felt about the same way, that it was an adventurous, fun time in their life, not the work they'd done especially, but just the experience of being on their own and being different, doing different work and everything.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: What made you leave the base?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Well, I got married out there, and then I had a child, and the war was ending so I had to quit. And then once you ever left there, see there were so many employees, you didn't get brought back on because it was, there were so many that wanted to stay and that could stay on full-time and, of course, see I was way across the country from it so it wasn't home to me and a lot of them that Utah was home to, they did stay on and work, some of them as along as they lived, cause the base is still there as I understand.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Have you ever been back?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I've been by there, I've never back on the base.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: When did you meet your husband?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I met him in 1944.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: On the base?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: On the base. He was stationed in the salvage yards, see they had stuff that was salvaged from use on the base, not just the planes, but from use on the base, and he worked in there because he was deferred from overseas duty on account of his feet. He had bone separation in his foot so he was discerned so he couldn't go overseas.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: How did you, how did the two of you meet?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Um, we met at a little drug store off from the base where we used to go and eat.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: You met at the drug store?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Hmm?

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: You met at the drug store?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: At the drugstore. They had a little lunch counter in there where you could get a soft drink and a sandwich and, of course, we'd all get tired of eating in the cafeteria and everything so we'd go down there after work and get us a sandwich and a soft drink...

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: And a husband.

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: And a husband, that's where a lot of us met.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Wow. Um, so how long were you on the base while you were with your husband?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: [pause] I'd say about six months.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: And you were, you got married in Utah?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Yes, we got married at the Army chapel in Utah.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: And um, would you still live in separate dorms after you were married?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: No, they had, by that time they had built apartment buildings for the married servicemen and their wives. Now if you were single, I think, you had to live, or just come out there and not married, you lived in the dorms, but you could get an apartment if you were married, off from the base, and it was very close, you could still walk to work. Cause like I said, there was no cars and there was no gas to run the cars if you had one.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: So then to get downtown would you walk?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: We'd walk up to where you'd catch the "elephant train."

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Oh, right. [pause] Oh, I know what I wanted to ask. Before you met your husband, what was the dating scene like?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Well, it was, you could date the servicemen out there, but I found that that was kind of risky dating cause you run into boys that were married, and they were boys , most of them were very young, that wouldn't tell you if they were married or not and so I mainly dated the boys that were, worked on the base, that were not married, some of them were maybe a year younger than I was, and there was really nowhere to date except to go on public transportation into Ogden and see a movie or something, that was the biggest thing we'd done. Then on the weekends, we would get on a bus and maybe go to Salt Lake City where they had big name bands come to their places, ballrooms I guess you call them. And we could dance and there was always a lot of servicemen there to dance with. And same way in Ogden. They had, I believe it was the White City in Ogden. Every weekend they would have dances. And I believe it was the Coconut Grove in Salt Lake City, and we'd just go there on the weekends, cause like I said, there was always somebody to dance with, and they encouraged the girls to go so that servicemen would have someone to dance with.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: And you were happy to go?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Yeah, we were happy to go, of course. Girls have always been girls, and boys have always been boys.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: [pause] You, when did you get pregnant?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Soon after I got married.

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Cause Eddie was born the first year after I got married.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Uh-huh. Could you have stayed on the base with a child?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Why did you decide to leave?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Because my husband was re-qualified for overseas duty and thought he was going overseas, but the first time he got as far as the Point of Embarkation, and it burned.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Where was that?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I think it was Seattle, Washington, and the second time, while he was on his way to the Point of Embarkation, they closed it down so he never did have to go overseas. But he thought he was having to go and so that was the reason that I left cause I didn't want to be left out there by myself.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Where would you have, would you have moved back home had he gone overseas?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: But he didn't, I know that you did not move back....

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Well, see the war was ending, too, and like I said, there was a lot of employees being laid-off. See the war ended in 1945. In fact, I was on the train going out there to visit him when the atomic bomb was dropped.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Going where, to Seattle?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: No, he was still in Utah.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: But he knew he was planning to go overseas so I was going out there to visit him, but during the time I was on the train, the atomic bomb was dropped and that ended the war with Japan.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Where were you visiting from, home in Minnesota?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: No, I was in North Carolina, and the war in Germany ended at the time my first child was born, I think I was in the hospital with him being born when the war in Germany ended.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Why did you, why did you move out to North Carolina?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Because he was coming home to North Carolina.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: And he...see as the war started coming down, they started letting the boys out of the Army, and he was high priority cause his mother was sick. And he was an only, he was an only son and so he had, and married and with a child so he had enough points to get out early.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Do you regret that you were taken, not that you were taken, it wasn't against your will, but that you left Utah because you were married?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I would like to have stayed in Utah, yes. I enjoyed it, the climate and the people, and I like Utah. We had made a lot of friends out there. Of course, you know, the friends were like we were, they were transient people.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Um, have you ever used any of your skills that you learned in the training in the rest of your life?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Nothing I don't think except my people skills of working with people. Cause there's no aircraft around here to repair. And I wasn't wealthy enough to own one.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Well, what did you spend the rest of your life as a career?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Mainly raising children. Well, no I first went to work in textile factories because I had no other experience and I worked in the textile factory for nine years and then when the college opened up here in Chadbourn, I went back to school and took accounting while I was working full-time as a textile worker and still had three children in school. And I don't know how I really made it because accounting is a hard subject but I did and then I got a job accounting. My first job was with a lady who had done home bookkeeping. She had an office, but she worked at home. Then I went to a hardware store, and then I went to the Anti-Poverage Program learned government bookkeeping which turned into a super responsible job. Well, when I started off, I think there was eleven employees total and one budget. When I ended up, there was about three hundred employees, and I had seventeen budgets to keep up with, and keep balances and everything, keep them going. And then when Head Start first came in, it came in as a summer program and no one in the whole organization knew how to run it, so since I was in charge of the money of it, I really had to do a lot towards getting that program off the ground. And it's still going strong here. So we had three counties of it. And it was just a summer program to start with.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: So you really never, all of the rest of your life, you did completely, completely different tasks?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: I had done accounting. And then I had done accounting for a multi-state tire corporation and had, which was also a big job because, like I said, covered three states, and I was in charge of all of the girls that were in that office doing secretarial work and had to look after the trucks that brought in the tires and were on the road all the time. I had to pay all their expenses, keep up with that, check all that, and keep a running balance at all times, and pay all the bills, in charge of all the payroll, had to sign the checks and make sure there was enough money to cover the checks.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Wow, well...

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: And then, after that, I went back to the Anti-Poverage Program. First off the man in the tire business, him and his wife separated, and he moved out of town and I didn't feel like I could move out of town because of family reasons and so I went back to the Anti-Poverage Program and went back as a planner which I had to do right much training for that. And then, let's see, the funding was stopped for that from the federal level and put on a state level and so I went in business for myself so I worked for the next twenty years, I guess, no, eighteen years, maybe twenty, I don't remember how long, in my own business doing income taxes and bookkeeping until my health got to where I couldn't do it anymore.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: And that brings us to today?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: That's till today, and now I sit at home and make quilts for my grandchildren and great-grandchildren.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Well, Grandma, I really appreciate this interview. Is there anything that you would like to say about your time during the war that I haven't covered?

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: My time during the war...well, at the time of the war, I grew up in a section of the country that was a farming section. There was not any industry. There was really not any jobs much that women could do without a college education, a teacher, a nurse or something. I grew up with family with eleven children, and we just did not have the money to go to college. It wasn't that we lacked the intelligence, we just didn't have the money, and so I guess that's the reason that I felt like I had to leave, well, I didn't feel like I had to leave either cause it was a loving family. We never felt unloved or neglected and we never felt poor because everybody else was just as poor or poorer than we were. But there was not the job opportunities there. It was about like your dad having to come back to Chadbourn to get a job. That was about the same as...or you having to come here and get a job. There wouldn't be much you could do. However, I never, never regretted that I've had a, I'd say an exciting life. I've traveled and done most of the things I've wanted to do.

sp.speaker: Claire Lanier
sp.p: Well, there you go. Thank you so much.

sp.speaker: Helen Lanier
sp.p: Thank you.
